title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8: Pontificii, Arminius, Remonstrants, Corvinus—efficacious grace hung on human consent
pass_a_gloss: But from the ancient Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians, let us descend to those who abominate the name of Pelagians, yet by no means turn away from the error. In this class I place those Papists who teach that grace is efficacious from the consent of the human will; so that if it happens that the will wills to assent, then God infuses vivifying grace, but if it resists, then the operation of God willing to vivify and regenerate the soul is rendered void. To these I also judge Arminius and the disciples of Arminius must be numbered, who so suspend the donation or negation of saving grace from human wills that they say God by absolute good pleasure wills to convert and regenerate no one, but wills to convert and regenerate all under the condition, if they themselves have not resisted his exciting grace, but to leave them unconverted if they have resisted. Thus the Remonstrants: If it is asked what the cause is why this one is converted, that one not, it is answered, This one is converted because God converts this one not opposing a new obstinacy; that one is not converted because he opposes a new obstinacy. Where from diverse acts of human choice they seek the reason of given and denied divine saving grace: but concerning God removing by special mercy the stony and obstinate heart, or not removing it by the liberty of his will, there is always deep silence among those people. So also Corvinus reduces whether we have or do not have that grace by which we are converted and saved not to the discrimination of the divine but of the human will. Against Bogerman, page 263: It is certain that nobody’s conversion is precisely intended by God. A little after: All the operations by which God uses to effect conversion in us having been posited, conversion nevertheless remains so in our power that we can not be converted. Thus stands the opinion of those people.
pass_b_english: From the old Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians we come down to people who hate the Pelagian name yet will not drop the error. In that class I put those Papists who teach that grace is efficacious by the consent of the human will: if the will happens to assent, God pours in vivifying grace; if it resists, God’s operation that would vivify and regenerate the soul is made void. With them I also count Arminius and his disciples, who hang the gift or denial of saving grace so far on human wills that they say God by absolute good pleasure wills to convert and regenerate no one, yet wills to convert and regenerate all on condition they have not resisted his exciting grace—and leaves them unconverted if they have resisted. So the Remonstrants: ask why this person is converted and that one is not, and the answer is that God converts the one who does not oppose with fresh obstinacy, and the other is not converted because he does oppose with fresh obstinacy. They take the reason for given or denied saving grace from different acts of human choice. About God removing the stony, stubborn heart by special mercy—or not removing it by the freedom of his own will—they keep a deep silence. Corvinus likewise refers whether we have or lack the grace by which we are converted and saved not to a discrimination of God’s will but of ours. Against Bogerman, p. 263: It is certain that nobody’s conversion is precisely intended by God. A little later: once all the operations God uses to work conversion in us are in place, conversion still remains so much in our power that we can refuse to be converted. That is their position.
source_text: Sed ab antiquis Pelagianis et Semipelagianis, ad eos descendamus qui nomen Pelagianorum abominantur, errorem tamen haud aversantur. In hac classe pono illos Pontificios qui docent gratiam esse efficacem a voluntatis humanae consensu; ita ut si contingat voluntatem velle assentire, tum Deus infundat gratiam vivificantem, sin ea resistat, tum operatio Dei volentis vivificare et regenerare animam irrita reddatur. Hisce etiam annumerandos sentio Arminium, et Arminii discipulos, qui gratiae salvantis donationem aut negationem ita suspendunt ab humanis voluntatibus, ut dicant, Deum ex absoluto beneplacito neminem velle convertere et regenerare, velle autem omnes convertere et regenerare sub conditione, si ipsi gratiae ejus excitanti non restiterint, relinquere autem inconverso, si restiterint. Sic Remonstrantes, Si quaeratur quae causa sit cur hic convertatur, ille non, respondetur, Hic convertitur, quia Deus hunc non opponentem novam contumaciam convertit; ille non convertitur, quia novam contumaciam opponit. Ubi ex diversis actibus humani arbitrii petunt rationem datae et negatae Divinae gratiae salutiferae: caeterum de Deo auferente per specialem misericordiam cor lapideum et contumax, aut non-auferente pro libertate voluntatis suae, altum semper apud istos silentium est. Sic etiam Corvinus, ut habeamus vel non habeamus eam gratiam qua convertimur et salvamur, non ad discrimen Divinae sed humanae voluntatis reducit. Contra Bogerman. pag. 263. Certum est nullius conversionem precise intendi a Deo. Paulo post, Positis omnibus operationibus quibus ad conversionem in nobis efficiendam Deus utitur, manet tamen conversio ita in nostra potestate ut possimus non converti. Sic se habet istorum sententia.
